speaker_role: former admissions reader (Dartmouth); now an independent counselor at InGenius Prep
commercial_incentive: channel promotes a free admissions consultation link; speaker currently works as a paid independent counselor
key_insights: Dartmouth admissions readers undergo intensive annual bias-awareness training in which each reader identifies their own personal biases (e.g., favoring Eagle Scouts), and every application gets at least two readers who know each other's individual biases.

Early decision applications get a more thorough, less rushed read simply because the pool is much smaller than regular decision, and Dartmouth has reportedly admitted close to half its incoming class through ED in recent years.
ED offers a real but not literally doubled admissions advantage and is recommended only when a school is a genuine first choice, given the binding financial commitment.

Under test-optional policy, submitted scores showed a slight statistical edge, particularly for international students or students from less-known/unusual high schools; the guidance is to submit only where scores land at or above the middle 50% range.

Readers reportedly review the activities list first (treating it as a compact personal essay), then transcript/honors, then essays, then recommendations and the required peer recommendation, which is meant to reveal informal personality rather than writing quality.

Common mistakes include naming a different school in the personal statement, writing in an overly formal/impressive voice instead of an authentic one, and submitting generic 'why school' essays that could apply to any similar college.
Waitlist movement is highly unpredictable year to year, and a letter of continued interest is valued for deferred or waitlisted applicants.

For younger students, activities should be chosen from genuine interest rather than strategy, and self-initiated community leadership (e.g., co-founding something with a peer) is seen as more distinctive than typical pre-existing school clubs.
specific_numbers_or_facts: An average Dartmouth admissions reader reviews over 1,000 applications per year, per Heather McCutchen
Dartmouth's ED round has recently comprised close to 50% of the incoming class, per McCutchen
Dartmouth's first supplemental essay is about 100 words; the second is 250-300 words with six topic options, per McCutchen
Dartmouth was announced test-optional through at least the 2022-2023 admissions cycle, per McCutchen
notable_or_distinctive: Gives an insider description of the reader-bias training process, where readers identify and disclose their own individual biases to fellow readers ahead of the season, a specific, non-generic detail rarely discussed publicly.
reliability_notes: Speaker explicitly no longer works there, and testing/essay-prompt policies change yearly, so some specifics may be outdated; the interview carries a commercial incentive from her current consulting role, though claims are framed as personal recollection rather than direct sales pitch.
